children: By Farhan Rafid and Anthony Harrup

Oil prices slipped back Friday after a string of gains, but ended the week sharply higher as traders assessed growing risks to Middle East crude exports from renewed fighting between the U.S. and Iran and fresh territorial gains made by Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen.

Front-month Brent crude oil settled down 2.8% at $104.61 a barrel, snapping a five-session winning streak but ending the week up 8.7%. Front-month West Texas Intermediate crude fell 2.4% to $100.05 a barrel after rising the previous eight sessions, and was up 9.4% on the week.

Friday's pullback marked a correction from an overbought condition, helped in part by reports that Oman is seeking a meeting with officials from Iran and other Gulf states to discuss shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, Dennis Kissler, senior vice president of trading at BOK Financial, said in a note.

Shipping around the Strait of Hormuz remained under pressure, with the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations saying Thursday that four unidentified projectiles struck two vessels near Khasab, Oman, causing a fire on one.

Meanwhile, Houthi militants captured the strategic port city of Mokha and Perim island, which sits inside the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and divides the narrow waterway into two shipping channels. That puts the group in a stronger position to threaten vessels entering or leaving the Red Sea.
Traders are more focused on Houthis gaining a foothold near the Bab al-Mandeb, Kissler said, "which gives them more areas to strike oil cargos."

Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on the route to circumvent disruptions in the Persian Gulf. The kingdom's crude production fell by roughly 1.9 million barrels a day to 6.24 million barrels a day in August, down 23% from July, according to the latest data from the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries.

The Saudi Energy Ministry said Friday that the East-West Pipeline used to transport oil to the Red Sea coast was shut down "as a precautionary measure" following several attacks on Thursday. The ministry said emergency teams took steps to secure the pipeline and assess its safety.
The pullback in crude followed a sharp rally Thursday, when WTI surged 6.7% and Brent gained 6.3% as intensifying fighting across the region fueled concerns over global energy supplies.

The International Energy Agency said Friday that a recovery in Middle East oil flows is now expected to stretch into next year as escalating attacks on Gulf shipping and Houthi threats in the Red Sea keep key energy arteries under strain.

The energy watchdog--formed by a group of Western nations and their allies--cut its outlook for global oil demand further, and now expects consumption to fall by 2.5 million barrels a day in 2026 to 102.4 million barrels a day, compared with its previous forecast for a 1.6-million barrel-a-day decline.
